characters: Abena: a curious thirteen-year-old Ghanaian girl in JHS 2, neat cornrow braids, wearing a bright yellow blouse and denim skirt.
Auntie Esi: Abena’s aunt in her thirties, a licensed investment advisor in Accra, wearing a tailored royal-blue blazer over a kente-print skirt and glasses.
Kwaku: Abena’s fourteen-year-old cousin, wearing a green polo shirt and carrying a calculator.

narrationPlan.voice: Clear, articulate Ghanaian narrator (en-GH); warm and authoritative for Auntie Esi, inquisitive for Abena and Kwaku.
narrationPlan.pace: Medium (about 120 words per minute); pause briefly around the portfolio calculations on pages 7–9.
notes: Pronounce Abena ("ah-BEH-nah"), Esi ("EH-see"), Kwaku ("KWAY-koo") and Accra ("uh-KRAH") clearly.

music: Optional subtle upright bass and soft Rhodes piano chords; off by default.
culturalNotes: References real Ghanaian capital-market institutions: the Ghana Stock Exchange (GSE) and the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC Ghana).
reviewQuestions: Are the distinctions between stocks, bonds, emergency savings, and Ponzi scams clear and age-appropriate for JHS 1–3?

pages.brief: Sunny Accra boulevard with modern glass-and-concrete buildings and tropical trees: Abena (13, cornrows, yellow blouse, denim skirt) and Kwaku (14, green polo shirt) looking up in curiosity as Auntie Esi (royal-blue blazer, glasses) gestures toward a commercial building.
pages.narration: Curious and engaging opening. Warm, knowledgeable tone from Auntie Esi.

pages.brief: Bright Accra advisory office: Auntie Esi at a whiteboard showing a colourful circular pie chart with one slice highlighted (no words or letters on the board), while Abena and Kwaku lean forward at the table.
pages.narration: Clear, vivid analogy of the pie divided into shares.

pages.brief: Close view at the office desk: Auntie Esi pointing to two visual diagram cards, one showing a factory sharing coins into a hand, the other showing a line chart going both up and down (no text).
pages.narration: Emphasise both ways stocks can earn returns AND the honest warning that neither is guaranteed.

pages.brief: Abena looking thoughtfully at a tablet screen showing a red line dipping downward and a blue line rising steadily (no text), while Auntie Esi speaks seriously beside her.
pages.narration: Measured, honest tone explaining capital loss and why short-term money must stay safe.

pages.brief: On the desk, two clear visual props side by side: a miniature factory building model (representing stock ownership) and a golden clock with coins beside a calendar (representing a fixed-term bond loan, no text).
pages.narration: Clear contrast: Stock = part-ownership; Bond = lending money for interest.

pages.brief: Thought bubble / tabletop visual comparison: Kwaku holding a coin pouch while looking at two market baskets, one full of books and fruit, the other only half full, illustrating how inflation shrinks what idle cash can buy.
pages.narration: Clear, relatable explanation of inflation and purchasing power.

pages.brief: Abena and Kwaku placing colourful wooden tokens into three separate small woven baskets on the desk: four tokens in Basket 1, two tokens in Basket 2, and four tokens in Basket 3 (no text labels).
pages.narration: Interactive, step-by-step setup of the 1,000-cedi diversified portfolio (400 + 200 + 400).

pages.brief: Kwaku pressing keys on a desktop calculator while Abena moves tokens: Basket 1 gains extra gold tokens, while Basket 2 loses a token.
pages.narration: Realistic simulation showing one stock gaining (+50) and one stock losing (-20).

pages.brief: Abena and Kwaku high-fiving across the desk as Auntie Esi points to the three baskets, two fuller than before, balancing out the smaller middle basket.
pages.narration: Walk through the arithmetic clearly: 450 + 180 + 460 = 1,090 cedis (+90 cedis / 9% return).

pages.brief: Close view: Kwaku holding up a smartphone showing a flashy warning icon (no text) while Auntie Esi raises a firm hand in a "stop" gesture and Abena shakes her head wisely.
pages.narration: Urgent, protective warning against Ponzi schemes and fraudulent "double your money" scams.

pages.brief: Warm family living room in Accra: Auntie Esi sitting with Abena, Kwaku and Abena’s parents, showing a clear glass emergency-savings jar beside an official folder with a gold seal (no text).
pages.narration: Practical, age-appropriate guidance on emergency funds first and parent/guardian accounts for minors.

pages.brief: Golden-hour view by a bus window: Abena smiling thoughtfully out at a vibrant Ghanaian cityscape with shops, solar rooftops and busy streets.

teacherGuide.overview: A rigorous, age-appropriate JHS financial literacy story introducing the Ghana Stock Exchange (GSE), the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC Ghana), stocks vs bonds, dividends, capital gains and losses, inflation, portfolio diversification, and anti-fraud vigilance.
learningGoals: Distinguish between stocks (equity ownership) and bonds (fixed-income lending).
Explain how dividends, capital gains, capital losses and inflation affect an investor’s purchasing power.
Calculate the total value and percentage return of a diversified portfolio (450 + 180 + 460 = 1,090 cedis on a 1,000-cedi initial investment = +9%).
Identify red flags of investment scams and explain the regulatory role of SEC Ghana and the need for adult/guardian accounts for minors.

beforeReading: Preview the title and cover illustration with learners and ask what real-world problem or question the characters might face.
whileReading: Pause at the embedded comprehension and vocabulary activities to check understanding and discuss the evidence in the text.
afterReading: Three-Basket Portfolio Maths: Give groups 10 paper "100-cedi" notes to allocate across three baskets (Stock A, Stock B, Bond) and compute the end-of-year value under different sunny and rainy economic cards.

Scam Detector Poster: Design a JHS poster listing SEC Ghana safety checks ("Is the firm licensed by SEC Ghana?", "Does it promise guaranteed instant doubling?", "Do I understand how the business makes money?").
discussion: If you buy shares in a company listed on the Ghana Stock Exchange, what does that make you, and what are the two ways you might earn a return?
Why did Auntie Esi include a losing stock (Company B dropping from 200 to 180 cedis) in the classroom simulation?
How does inflation quietly shrink money kept idle in a box over many years?
What three warning signs show that an online "investment" offer is actually a scam or Ponzi scheme?

whatWeKnow: In Ghana, the Ghana Stock Exchange (GSE) provides the regulated marketplace for listed equities and corporate/government debt securities, while the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC Ghana) regulates and licenses capital-market operators.
Diversification across uncorrelated assets reduces portfolio volatility compared with holding a single stock.
whatWeAreStillDiscovering: Financial economists study how mobile-based regulated micro-investing platforms can safely expand capital-market participation in West Africa while screening out unlicensed schemes.

investigation.title: One Basket vs Three Baskets Simulation
materials: Ten counters (representing 100 cedis each = 1,000 cedis), three cups labelled Stock A, Stock B, and Bond, and a coin to flip.
steps: Scenario 1 (Undiversified): Put all 10 counters (1,000 cedis) into Stock B alone. When Stock B drops by 10%, calculate your ending total (900 cedis, a 100-cedi loss).
Scenario 2 (Diversified): Place 4 counters in Stock A (+12.5% → 450 cedis), 2 counters in Stock B (-10% → 180 cedis), and 4 counters in Bond (+15% → 460 cedis).
Add the three cups in Scenario 2 (450 + 180 + 460 = 1,090 cedis) and compare with Scenario 1.

pronunciation.guidance: Ghanaians often say "uh-KRAH" (stress on the second syllable).

reviewerNotes: Confirm first syllable vowel (kway vs kwah).
